message.reasoning:
I need to make a Monopoly decision.

I'm analyzing my holdings. I have $579 cash and am on ILLINOIS_AVENUE. The dark blue properties are fully upgraded with 4 houses each, so hotels are possible. The red properties have 1 to 2 houses. Several light blue properties remain mortgaged.

Player 1 is bankrupt. Player 3 has $306 and all properties mortgaged. Player 4 has $163 and shares my position on ILLINOIS_AVENUE with a brown monopoly, railroads, utilities, yellows, and a GOOJF card. The bank holds 11 houses and 12 hotels.

Atlantic and Pacific are unowned. Player 4 has roughly $1193 in cash. A hotel on Park Place would cost $200 and raise rent from $1100 to $1500. A hotel on Boardwalk would cost $200 and raise rent from $1400 to $2000.

Standard rent tables confirm the prior figures. A hotel on Park Place would raise rent by only $200, matching its $200 construction cost.

Boardwalk hotels would raise rent by $300 for the same $200 cost. Hotels do not improve the kill shot against current opponents because both properties already bankrupt them. They reduce cash buffer instead. The next step is to assess what could hurt me, since turn 82 is my post-turn action.

Player 3 and player 4 will take turns next. Player 1 is bankrupt and skipped. Player 4 already paid rent on Illinois Avenue this turn, so they will not pay again until they leave and return. The main risk is landing on player 4's properties.

Player 4's brown properties are fully upgraded with four houses each. Mediterranean Avenue now charges $160 in rent, and Baltic Avenue charges $320. The pink monopoly is broken because St. Charles Place is mortgaged, so Oriental and Virginia only pay base rent.

Player 4 owns Reading Railroad and Pennsylvania Railroad. He also owns Electric Company and Water Works, which charge ten times the dice roll. Marvin Gardens is his only yellow property; Ventnor is mortgaged.

Player 4 has no yellow or green monopoly. He owns only brown properties, two railroads, and utilities. From Illinois Avenue, the next spaces are B&O Railroad, Atlantic, Ventnor, Water Works, Marvin Gardens, Go to Jail, Pacific, North Carolina, and Community Chest.

I mapped the full board from Illinois Avenue. A roll of five lands on Water Works, which charges ten times the dice roll. Marvin Gardens costs $24 in base rent. Pennsylvania Avenue and Short Line are mine and mortgaged. The next spaces are Chance, Park Place, Luxury Tax, and Boardwalk.

The nearest danger is Water Works, which charges $50. Marvin Gardens and North Carolina are also reachable but pay only $24 and $26. Luxury Tax is too far away to hit this turn. Player 4's brown properties are out of reach for now.

My cash of $579 is safe against these small rent amounts. I am not on a Chance or Community Chest space right now, so I cannot be moved by those cards until next turn.

Building hotels would cost $200 each. That would drop my cash to about $179, but it still leaves enough buffer for the next roll. I should also remember that a "Make general repairs" card costs $25 per house and $100 per hotel.

This game charges $40 per house for repairs. Converting four houses to a hotel would leave nine houses and one hotel, costing $475 in repairs. Standard deluxe rates are $25 per house and $100 per hotel.

A hotel repair cost of $100 would total $460. The current $520 repair bill leaves only a $59 buffer. Adding a house to Kentucky Avenue would raise repairs to $560 and leave cash at $429, which is unsafe if a "Make general repairs" card is drawn. Hotels do not improve the kill shot against current opponents because both properties already bankrupt them.

Player 3 cannot unmortgage all three orange properties with only $306. Player 4 has $163 and a brown monopoly with four houses, so he might want to build hotels or buy unowned properties. I am now considering whether to trade.

I am weighing a trade to strip player 4 of his brown monopoly or acquire dangerous properties from him. My light blue properties are all mortgaged, so unmortgaging them would complete a monopoly. The cost to unmortgage Vermont Avenue is $55 and Connecticut Avenue is $66.

Unmortgaging all three light blue properties costs $198, leaving about $381 for construction. Even fully upgraded, light blue rents are too weak to threaten player 4, who is already bankrupted by the dark blue properties. The cash would be better spent elsewhere.

Player 3 is on St. Charles Place. Neither player can reach Park Place or Boardwalk from their current positions in a single turn, since the distance exceeds twelve spaces. The light blue properties would only be reachable via Chance cards.

Neither opponent can pay rent to me next turn. Player 3 on St. Charles Place cannot reach any of my mortgaged properties from rolls of two through twelve. Player 4 on Illinois Avenue also cannot reach any of my mortgaged properties from those rolls. The only spaces they might land on are their own utilities and possibly unowned Atlantic or Pacific. I will not hit their dangerous properties next turn either. The game continues.

I am now considering building houses on the red properties. Only Kentucky Avenue is buildable, and its rent would rise to $250 with two houses. This would bankrupt player 4 when they eventually land there.

Player 4's total liquidity is roughly $1193, so a $250 rent on Kentucky Avenue would bankrupt him. Player 3 has only $306, which would not kill him. I am now calculating how much cash player 4 could raise by selling his eight brown houses and mortgaging his properties.

Player 4's total liquid assets are roughly $1,193. A $250 rent on Kentucky Avenue would not bankrupt him; he could sell his eight brown houses to survive. Building two houses there would cost $150 and force him to de-house his brown properties if he lands. This is a defensive move rather than an immediate kill shot.

Player 4 cannot reach Kentucky Avenue from Illinois in a single turn. Building two houses on Kentucky would raise its rent to $250 and match Indiana and Illinois at two houses each. The engine allows another action, so I could build all three red properties to three houses next. That would raise rent on Kentucky to $700, Indiana to $700, and Illinois to $850.

Even fully upgraded red properties cannot bankrupt player 4. Their total liquid assets are roughly $1,193, and the highest red rent is only about $1,100. Player 4 would survive by selling buildings and mortgaging properties. The dark blue monopoly remains the only real threat.

Building two houses on the red properties would cost only $150. Indiana and Illinois would then charge $250 and $300, which kills player 3 but not player 4. Player 4 could survive by selling his brown houses to pay the rent. This would reduce player 4's brown threat while adding bankruptcy spaces for player 3.

I cannot build three houses on all red properties because that would cost $600, and I only have $579. Even upgrading Kentucky to two houses costs $150, leaving me with $429. Player 3 has only $306, so the $250 rent from two houses on Kentucky would not bankrupt him. Player 4 is already safe from the current $300 rent on Illinois Avenue with two houses. This upgrade is too marginal to be worthwhile.

Building red properties now would waste the cash and erode the repair buffer. Unmortgaging the light blue properties costs $198, but even fully upgraded they would only kill player 3. Player 4 is already safe from light blue rent. This makes the light blue route unattractive.

Player 4's four houses on Baltic and Mediterranean Avenue would cost $320 and $160 in rent. That is the only remaining serious threat. I am now considering a trade to acquire his brown monopoly or force him to give up those houses.

Player 4 cannot bankrupt me with his current brown houses. Even a hotel on Baltic Avenue would cost $450, which I can still afford with $579 cash. Hoteling both browns would leave him with only $63, yet I could still pay the rent. The brown monopoly is not an immediate threat.

Player 4's brown monopoly is already maxed at four houses, so hotels cannot increase the threat further. Player 3 poses no danger because every property is mortgaged. The safest path is to end the turn and let the other players walk into my dark blue properties. A trade for player 4's Get Out of Jail Free card would be useless since I am not in jail. Buying his Baltic and Mediterranean Avenue would remove the last serious threat, but he would demand a large price for that four-house monopoly.

I realized that player 4 already owns all three pink properties, so he cannot complete another pink monopoly. I also decided not to give him cash, since even a small sum would let him survive a dark blue rent hit.

Player 4 cannot unmortgage St. Charles Place because he lacks the $77 mortgage cost. He also cannot build houses on the pink properties, since each house costs $100 and he has only $163 after paying the mortgage. The pink monopoly remains harmless for now.

Player 3's orange properties are all mortgaged. Acquiring them would require roughly $308 to unmortgage plus house costs, and the rent income is strong. Player 3 has only $306, so any cash I give him would let him survive the $300 rent on Illinois Avenue with two houses. I must be careful about what I offer in a trade.

I am now considering whether to build hotels on the red properties. Player 4 could pass Go and collect $200, raising his liquidity to roughly $1,393. That would make the $1,300 rent on Park Place no longer bankrupt him. Building hotels now would increase rent income in case he gains cash before landing.

Hoteling Park Place would raise its rent to $1,500. Player 4 could still afford this after passing Go and collecting $200, so the threat remains. He cannot pass Go from Illinois in one turn; he needs 16 spaces, which is impossible with a roll of 12. Player 3 is roughly 29 spaces from Go and would need at least two turns to reach it.

Player 3 cannot raise enough cash to survive a dark blue rent hit. Even after passing Go twice, he would still have only about $706, which is below the $1,300 needed to survive Park Place. Player 4 could survive a single Go pass and reach roughly $1,393, but he would still be bankrupted by Boardwalk or a hotel on Park Place.

Hoteling both red properties would cost $400 and leave only $179. That is too little to survive a Baltic Avenue rent of $320, so I would have to sell buildings anyway. The defensive upgrade is not worthwhile.

Building one hotel on Park Place would leave $59 after paying Baltic Avenue rent, which is enough to survive without selling buildings. Boardwalk already has a large margin, so the extra cash from a second hotel would be wasted. The better upgrade is only the Park Place hotel.

I am checking the exact mechanics of selling a hotel back to houses. In Monopoly, a hotel must be replaced with four houses if available; otherwise it sells for half its cost and leaves the property at zero houses. The bank currently holds 19 houses and 12 hotels. Building two hotels would return eight houses to the bank.

Selling a hotel back to houses is risky. It returns only half the cost and may force a downgrade to four houses. I will not build both hotels because that would leave me with only $179, which is too little to pay Baltic Avenue rent of $320 without selling buildings. Building one hotel on Park Place is safe because $379 remains above the $320 threshold. A second hotel on Boardwalk is less strategic since it already kills player 4.

Unmortgaging Vermont Avenue for $55 would leave only $324 after building a Park Place hotel. That is still below the $320 rent on Baltic Avenue, so it would not help. The light blue properties are all mortgaged, and unmortgaging one does not yet create a monopoly rent. This path offers no benefit.

I am now calculating the exact repair cost of building a hotel on Park Place. The current assessment is $520 for 13 houses at $40 each. Hoteling one property would reduce the house count to nine and add one hotel, which changes the total repair bill.

I am weighing the exact repair cost of building a hotel on Park Place. If the house rate is $40 and the hotel rate is $115, the total repair bill would be $475. That exceeds my remaining cash of $379 by $96, which could force me to sell buildings and drop Boardwalk below its kill rent. If the rates are instead $25 and $100, the total would be $325, which I can afford. I still need to confirm which card version applies.

I will end the turn without building a hotel. The $59 cash buffer is too small to cover a potential $475 repair bill if I add a hotel, and selling houses would weaken my kill shot. I will not spend the repair buffer.

messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

Roll; only leave on doubles. Keep Vermont mortgaged.

Jail turn 1, $280, BW3 ($1400)/PP2 ($500). Paying $50 puts me on the board toward p3 oranges and p1 reds ($250/$300) and p4 Baltic ($320) — any of those forces a BW house sale and kills the win rent. Nobody can reach PP/BW before my next turn (p1/p3 on B&O need 12 for PP only; p4 jailed, can't reach dark blue even on doubles chains). Rent still collects here. Roll; leave only if doubles. Keep Vermont mortgaged.
